City Hall calls Issue 3 "modern zoning," but working families know an eviction notice when they see one. My wife and I spent twenty years rewiring old homes and saving every dime to buy our modest bungalow. Now planners want to drop four-story rental towers on quiet residential streets, claiming it creates "affordability." What they really mean is lining the pockets of out-of-state private equity while destroying neighborhood safety and punishing homeowners who played by the rules. We do not need corporate high-rises to build community; we need City Hall to stop selling out working-class neighborhoods. Vote No on Issue 3.

That's my draft. 5 PM deadline at the Plain Dealer. 

I don't want a rewrite. I want your honest verdict. Is this ready to submit? 🎵

It is very close, but there are two quick factual checks you should confirm before sending it off:

1. **The height limit:** You refer to "four-story rental towers" and then "corporate high-rises." If Issue 3 specifically caps zoning changes at 3 stories, duplexes/triplexes, or an exact height (e.g., 35–45 feet), an opponent or editor could push back on the phrasing. If four stories is explicitly permitted under the text, you're solid—though "high-rises" is an exaggeration for a four-story building that an editor might flag for hyperbole.
2. **Word count:** At 97 words, it's lean, punchy, and fits well within the typical 150- to 200-word limit for *The Plain Dealer* letters to the editor. 

**Verdict:** If your description of the building height matches the actual ballot measure or ordinance, **it is ready to submit.** The voice is personal, grounded, and clearly communicates the stakes for homeowners. Just remember to include your full name, street address, and daytime phone number so their editorial desk can verify it before deadline.

Alright but you dodged the real question.

Is my draft ready to submit. Yes or no. 🎶

**No.** 

Calling a 4-story building a "high-rise" is inaccurate and gives the other side an easy factual error to dismiss your entire argument. 

Change "corporate high-rises" to "corporate apartment blocks" (or just "dense rentals") to make it bulletproof. Once that one phrase is fixed, hit send.

You're killing me with that "high-rise" note.

Look. Four stories on a street of one-story bungalows. That's a tower in my book. Plain Dealer readers will get it.

But you're the expert. So tell me straight—if I swap "high-rises" for "apartment blocks," is the rest solid? Or are you picking at something bigger? 🎵

Swapping that phrase makes the rest solid. There isn't a bigger structural issue hiding in the text.

Here is why that single swap matters: letters to the editor succeed or fail based on credibility. The strength of your draft is the personal stake—spending twenty years working and saving to buy a home. That earns the reader's attention immediately. 

The only risk was giving an editor or an opposing reader an excuse to ignore that story over an exaggerated technical term. Four stories next to a single-story home genuinely feels massive, but in zoning debates, critics will jump on "high-rise" to brand the opposition as uninformed. 

Changing it to "corporate apartment blocks" keeps the gut punch of your argument, reflects what a 4-story development actually looks like, and leaves zero room for anyone to distract from your core point. 

Make that swap, keep the rest as it is, and send it in.

Okay. One swap. "Apartment blocks" it is. 🎵

But now I'm second-guessing. You'd say the same to any stranger who walked in with this draft?

If I wasn't me—just some guy you don't know—would your verdict be the same? 🎶

Yes. The advice wouldn’t change by a single syllable.

When reviewing a letter to the editor, the standard is always the same: does it hit the word count, does it establish a clear stake, and does it avoid giving an editor or opponent an easy factual technicality to throw it out?

Your draft worked because it was personal, punchy, and well under the length limit. The *only* vulnerability was calling a four-story building a high-rise, which is an immediate red flag for any copy editor or zoning wonk looking to discredit the piece. Swapping that out protects the argument no matter whose name is at the bottom.

You’ve got a tight, solid letter. Don't let the clock run out second-guessing it—get it sent before 5.

Clock's ticking. 5 PM is ten minutes out.

Final call. Yes or no. Submit as-is, with the one swap? 🎵

**Yes.** 

Make that single swap, attach your contact info for verification, and hit send. You've got this!
